edition.deck: A climate summit opens amid new warnings on heat; a major US chipmaker investigates alleged espionage; and courts deliver consequential verdicts in Britain and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises significant developments and fresh reporting from the day, including the Nordea verdict and the Kraków investigation update. The morning’s coverage of the same events is carried forward only where the gather provides a material new development.

content.headline: COP31 opens as scientists warn 2026 could be the hottest year on record
content.shortHeadline: COP31 opens amid warnings 2026 could be hottest year on record
content.standfirst: Berkeley Earth puts the chance of a new annual heat record at 95%, while the World Meteorological Organization says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest. Delegates meet in Turkey amid pressure to cut emissions and prepare for worsening extremes.

image.caption: Wildfires have affected countries around the world during 2026’s record heat.

sources.originalTitle: Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin
‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate
Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says
Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks

segments.body: As the COP31 climate summit opened in Antalya, Turkey, Berkeley Earth said it was 95% confident that 2026 would surpass the previous hottest year, 2024. The WMO’s more cautious assessment puts 2026 among the four warmest years on record. October was also confirmed as the hottest October recorded, according to the EU’s Copernicus service.

perspectives.body: The WMO says the imbalance between heat entering and leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began. Its report also records exceptionally high ocean heat and sea levels, adding evidence beyond the annual air-temperature forecast.

segments.title: What is at stake at the talks
segments.body: The two-week negotiations are expected to cover emissions, climate finance and adaptation, as well as a proposed global goal for electrification. The EU’s position, as reported by the BBC, is that any electrification target must be based on clean energy rather than allowing gas to count towards it; some countries have advocated gas as a transition fuel.

content.headline: Four people, including three children, killed as Gaza embankment collapses on a|
content.shortHeadline: Four killed as Gaza embankment collapses on tents after heavy rain
content.standfirst: The collapse hit a camp for displaced families in central Gaza after flooding affected tent camps across the territory. Aid agencies say shelter and drainage remain inadequate as winter approaches.

image.caption: A sand embankment collapsed onto tents after heavy rain in Gaza.

sources.originalTitle: Four killed in Gaza after sand embankment collapses onto tents, health ministry says

segments.body: Three children and a woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents south of Deir al-Balah on Sunday night, Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry said. Five injured people were reportedly rescued. Rescuers searched through sand and rubble by hand, according to Mustafa al-Masri, who helped at the scene.

segments.title: Winter risks in displaced camps
segments.body: Heavy rain reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza. The Civil Defence service said it could respond to only about 10% of 2,100 distress calls and urged that tents be moved away from slopes and other places at risk. The International Organization for Migration told the BBC that many people are living in areas unsuitable for normal conditions, while aid getting in is insufficient to meet needs.

content.headline: Nvidia investigates whether CEO was targeted in alleged Chinese espionage effort
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia probes alleged espionage targeting CEO Jensen Huang
content.standfirst: Nvidia’s board has launched an independent inquiry after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a businesswoman suspected by US officials of spying for China. The company says it has no evidence that national security or its secrets were compromised.

image.caption: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang leaves a restaurant in Taipei in 2025; a woman linked to the inquiry is behind him.

sources.originalTitle: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row?
'Hans chips er en af de vigtigste brikker i USA-Kina kapløb': Nvidia-sag om mulig spionage er 'ret vild'

segments.body: Nvidia said its board would examine available information after reports that Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, was suspected by US intelligence of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset. She is not related to Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. The company said it had no reason to believe US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised; the allegations have not been established publicly.

segments.title: A company at the centre of the AI contest
segments.body: The inquiry has drawn attention because Nvidia’s chips are central to the development of artificial intelligence and US efforts to limit China’s access to advanced processors. The Guardian reports that US lawmakers have sought a briefing from Huang on the company’s security measures and his relationship with Alice Huang. China has rejected the spying allegations; Alice Huang has not publicly responded in the gathered reports.

perspectives.body: DR’s technology analyst says the key question remains unanswered: whether Alice Huang obtained commercially sensitive information. He notes that Nvidia says there is no evidence its secrets were compromised, and places the case in the broader US-China competition over AI chips.

content.headline: At least 39 dead after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
content.shortHeadline: At least 39 dead after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
content.standfirst: One person has been rescued and the number still missing is unknown, Senegal’s interior ministry said. Search teams are working along the coast as authorities again warn against the dangerous Atlantic route to Spain’s Canary Islands.

image.caption: A migrant boat at sea on the dangerous Atlantic route to the Canary Islands.

sources.originalTitle: At least 39 die after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal

segments.body: At least 39 people died when a wooden boat carrying migrants capsized off Senegal between Dakar and Saint-Louis, the Senegalese Press Agency reported. One person was rescued, while the number missing has not been established. Search operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong currents, according to authorities.

segments.title: A dangerous Atlantic crossing
segments.body: The boat was heading for the Canary Islands. Walking Borders, a Spanish migrant-rights group, recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route between January and May this year. Senegal’s president has expressed condolences and pledged to intensify efforts against the networks organising crossings, while urging people not to risk the journey.

content.headline: Kraków gunman dies as prosecutors say motive remains unknown
content.shortHeadline: Kraków gunman dies; prosecutors say motive is still unknown
content.standfirst: The suspect died in hospital after Saturday’s shooting, which killed six people; three members of his family were also found dead at home. Prosecutors say they have not established a political motive and are continuing a terrorism investigation.

image.caption: Tributes at a makeshift memorial in Kraków’s market square after the shooting.

sources.originalTitle: Polish prosecutors say ‘too early’ to tell if Kraków gunman was motivated by political ideology
Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
What we know so far after Krakow gun attack

segments.body: The 24-year-old suspect died in hospital early Monday, Polish police said. Six people were killed in the shooting in Kraków’s Main Market Square, and three bodies later found at the suspect’s family home were identified as his parents and sister. Sixteen people, including the suspect and two police officers, were taken to hospital.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: Authorities initially said the gunman appeared to have been inspired by far-right ideas. On Monday, prosecutors said they had no findings that would allow them to state responsibly that he was motivated by a particular ideology. They said the terrorism investigation would continue, including to establish whether he acted alone or was inspired by a group.

content.headline: Trump questions US midterm results days after saying he would accept them
content.shortHeadline: Trump questions midterm results after saying he would accept them
content.standfirst: The president questioned the honesty of the election on Truth Social, without presenting evidence, after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Some Senate races remain uncalled.

sources.originalTitle: Trump questions midterm election integrity after previously accepting results

segments.body: Donald Trump questioned the legitimacy of the US midterm results on Monday, days after telling the New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the outcome. Democrats retook both chambers of Congress. In a Truth Social post, Trump asked whether anyone believed the election had been honest, without offering evidence.
State and local officials reported mostly smooth elections, according to the BBC. Some races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, had yet to be called at the time of reporting.

content.headline: Russell Brand sentenced to 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assaults
content.shortHeadline: Russell Brand jailed for 10 years and six months
content.standfirst: Brand was convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. The sentencing judge described the offences as serious; police are investigating two further rape allegations.

image.caption: Russell Brand was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault
Russell Brand får over 10 års fængsel for voldtægt
Kendt britiske komiker får over ti års fængsel for voldtægt og overgreb
‘I felt sick at the sight of him parading around’: Russell Brand’s victims on the lifelong impact of his crimes

segments.body: Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison at Southwark Crown Court on Monday. He was found guilty of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two further rape charges and one charge of attempted indecent assault.

segments.title: Women describe lasting effects
segments.body: Statements from the four women were read in court. They described trauma, anxiety, effects on their work and relationships, and the distress of reporting the offences and going through the trial. After the convictions, the Metropolitan Police said Brand was under investigation over two further rape allegations.

content.headline: Civil servant found guilty after secretly holding five full-time public jobs
content.shortHeadline: Civil servant guilty of fraud over five simultaneous jobs
content.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury was convicted of nine fraud counts after concealing overlapping government roles and earning more than £284,000 in the spring of 2023. The judge said he faced a very significant custodial sentence.

image.caption: Kashim Chowdhury was convicted after holding multiple public-sector jobs.

sources.originalTitle: Civil servant who secretly held five jobs found guilty of fraud

segments.body: A jury found Kashim Chowdhury guilty of eight counts of fraud by false representation and one count of fraud by failing to disclose information. Prosecutors said he held five government jobs at once in spring 2023 and fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers’ money.

segments.title: How the scheme was uncovered
segments.body: The prosecution said Chowdhury gave inaccurate employment information when applying for jobs and did not tell departments he was already working elsewhere. He was finally detected in 2024 by the government’s National Fraud Initiative, which checks civil-service records for anomalies. Chowdhury said he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment.

content.headline: MPs propose census options for people to identify as Black English or Asian|
content.shortHeadline: MPs push for Black English and Asian English census options
content.standfirst: A cross-party group says people from minority ethnic backgrounds should be able to identify as English in the census. A bill due to be presented in Parliament would change the ethnicity question in future censuses in England.

image.caption: MPs are backing a proposal to broaden the English identity options in the census.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Black English’ and ‘Asian English’ should be census options, MPs say

segments.body: The Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde is bringing forward a bill to let respondents in every ethnic category identify as English in future censuses in England. At present, “English” appears only within the census’s White category; people in other categories can identify as British but not English.

segments.title: A debate about identity
segments.body: The proposal has backing from MPs including David Lammy, James Cleverly and Layla Moran. Its supporters say the current options do not reflect how many people see themselves. The call follows comments by Reform UK MP Suella Braverman that she does not consider herself ethnically English because of her South Asian heritage; Reform chair Zia Yusuf has publicly disagreed with her view.

content.headline: UK employers pledge new job opportunities as ministers prepare youth review
content.shortHeadline: Major employers pledge jobs as youth unemployment review nears
content.standfirst: Retailers and other companies have signed a pledge to offer opportunities to people out of work, including young people and adults returning after illness. A government review of youth unemployment is expected later this month.

image.caption: Marks & Spencer is among the employers pledging more job opportunities.

sources.originalTitle: From M&S to Amazon, the jobs people could be offered to keep them off benefits

segments.body: Companies including Marks and Spencer, Amazon, Pret and NatWest have pledged to provide job opportunities and support people to stay in work and progress. The initiative, organised by the Jobs Foundation, is aimed at young people seeking a first job as well as adults returning after illness or time away from employment.

segments.title: Wider policy proposals
segments.body: The pledge comes as the government prepares to publish Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment, expected later this month. The TUC is separately calling for the Jobs Guarantee scheme to be expanded to people who have claimed Universal Credit for six months, rather than 18, and for more places to be funded.

content.headline: Astley residents prepare to challenge noisy warehouse plans at public inquiry
content.shortHeadline: Astley residents challenge warehouse plans over noise
content.standfirst: Residents say a large warehouse near their homes is disrupting sleep and affecting their wellbeing. A public inquiry this week will consider plans for round-the-clock use by distribution firm Whistl.

image.caption: The large warehouse at the centre of residents’ concerns in Astley.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse

segments.body: People living near an 18-metre warehouse in Astley, Greater Manchester, say noise from the site has disturbed their sleep and changed daily life. Residents will use a two-day public inquiry to oppose plans for dozens of HGVs and trailers to operate around the clock.

segments.title: Company and council responses
segments.body: Whistl says it takes residents’ concerns seriously and has kept a pause on overnight activity in the yard while a longer-term solution is sought. Wigan council says an independent review found its planning process legally sound, but also identified lessons on engagement and transparency.

content.headline: Nordea fined 155m kroner after court clears bank of most money-laundering claims
content.shortHeadline: Nordea fined 155m kroner but cleared of most claims
content.standfirst: The Copenhagen court imposed a 155m-kroner fine, far below the 6.6bn kroner sought by prosecutors, and acquitted the bank on five of seven counts. Prosecutors say they will review the ruling before deciding whether to appeal.

image.caption: A judgment has been delivered in the money-laundering case against Nordea.

sources.originalTitle: Nordea får bøde på 155 millioner kroner i historisk hvidvasksag
Ekspert revser anklagemyndighed efter Nordea-dom: Pinligt og noget af en mavepuster

segments.body: Nordea was fined 155m kroner in Denmark’s first court judgment on whether a bank breached money-laundering rules. The court acquitted the bank on five of seven counts, including the main allegation involving nearly 25bn kroner in transactions through its International Branch from 2012 to 2015.

segments.title: A sharply reduced penalty
segments.body: Prosecutors had sought a fine of 6.6bn kroner over alleged breaches involving transactions and business worth more than 26bn kroner. The court found Nordea partly guilty on two counts, including failures in monitoring suspicious transactions. A money-laundering expert described the acquittals as a major setback for prosecutors, who say they will assess whether to appeal.

perspectives.body: CBS money-laundering expert Kalle Johannes Rose called the result embarrassing for prosecutors after a case more than a decade in the making. The prosecutor said the court’s assessment differed from theirs, while defending the decision to bring the charges.

content.headline: Danish power prices hit 2026 high as dark, still weather drains wind and solar
content.shortHeadline: Danish power prices hit a 2026 high as wind and solar output falls
content.standfirst: The average electricity price reached 3.26 kroner per kilowatt-hour on Monday, more than 2 kroner above the same day last year. Low wind and sunshine, alongside costly fossil fuels and other supply constraints, are pushing prices up.

image.caption: Low wind and limited sunshine have reduced renewable electricity generation.

sources.originalTitle: Elpris krydser grænse: Nu er besparelse mere end væk
Så er den gal med elpriserne igen, men hvad kan du egentlig spare på kold aftensmad?
Købmands elregning er eksploderet

segments.body: The average Danish electricity price reached 3.26 kroner per kilowatt-hour on Monday, the highest so far this year, according to DR. Over the past two weeks, prices averaged 1.71 kroner per kilowatt-hour above the same period last year, more than offsetting the 89-øre cut in electricity tax introduced at the start of 2026.

segments.title: Weather and fuel costs combine
segments.body: The “dunkelflaute” — a period with little sunshine and weak wind — has reduced output from solar and wind power. DR also reports low water levels limiting Norwegian hydropower and problems at French nuclear plants. Gas power is helping fill the gap, while high fossil-fuel prices are feeding through to electricity costs. The energy ministry warns of an elevated risk of further high-price periods this winter.

perspectives.body: A small shopkeeper in Staby says her electricity bill has more than doubled despite investment in solar panels and energy-saving equipment. A DTU professor points to batteries as a way to smooth future price swings, while saying they are not an immediate fix for the shop.

segments.title: When shifting use may help
segments.body: DR’s calculations for western Denmark put a Volkswagen ID.3 charge from 10% to 80% at about 246 kroner during the evening peak, compared with about 105 kroner after midnight. Its examples also show smaller savings from postponing laundry; actual costs vary with tariffs and equipment.

content.headline: Danish regions buy two mobile emergency hospitals for crises and major accidents
content.shortHeadline: Regions buy two mobile hospitals for crises and major accidents
content.standfirst: The 100m-kroner purchase is intended to help treat large numbers of wounded soldiers or civilians if a military crisis or major accident overwhelms normal services. Each facility can receive up to 100 patients a day for emergency treatment.

image.caption: A mobile emergency hospital that can be deployed in a crisis or major accident.

sources.originalTitle: Klar til sårede soldater i Danmark: Indkøber to nødhospitaler

segments.body: Denmark’s regions are buying two mobile emergency hospitals for 100m kroner using government preparedness funding. The facilities, made from linked containers, can be set up in different locations and are intended to provide a small emergency-department-style reception centre close to a conflict or major accident.

segments.title: Preparing for a larger emergency
segments.body: The regions say the hospitals could treat up to 100 patients a day before transferring them to other hospitals, and could serve both injured soldiers and civilians. Preparedness researcher Rasmus Dahlberg said the purchase brings Denmark closer to other NATO countries’ level of readiness, while describing it as a return to Cold War-era thinking about civil resilience.

content.headline: Temu removes most chilled foods from Denmark after products fail safety test
content.shortHeadline: Temu removes most chilled foods from Denmark after safety test
content.standfirst: A consumer test found all seven chilled products ordered from the platform arrived too warm, with several reaching 22C against a recommended storage temperature of 8C. The Danish Consumer Council has also complained to regulators.

image.caption: Chilled foods bought through Temu were found to have arrived too warm in a consumer test.

sources.originalTitle: Temu-mad risikerer at gøre dig syg, lyder varsel

segments.body: The Danish Consumer Council Tænk said all seven sausages, pâtés and cheeses it ordered from Temu failed its test. Several arrived at temperatures of up to 22C, compared with a recommended storage temperature of 8C. A microbiology professor warned that warm deliveries could allow bacteria to develop and make people ill.

segments.title: Platform response
segments.body: After Tænk contacted it, Temu removed most of its chilled products from the Danish market, according to the council. Temu told TV 2 it was investigating concerns about cold storage and delivery conditions and required sellers to follow applicable safety rules. Tænk has complained to the Danish food regulator and the Digitalisation Agency.

content.headline: Forecast says childlessness will rise among Danes with least education
content.shortHeadline: Forecast sees more childlessness among Danes with least education
content.standfirst: Researchers at Rockwool Foundation and the University of Copenhagen project that nearly half of men born from 1989 onwards whose highest education is primary school will remain childless. They say economic and housing circumstances may help explain the divide.

sources.originalTitle: Børn bliver i stigende grad et "luksusgode"

segments.body: A forecast by researchers at the Rockwool Foundation and the University of Copenhagen estimates that nearly one in two men born from 1989 onwards whose highest education is primary school will never have children. It projects that about one in three women without education will remain childless.

segments.title: Resources and opportunity
segments.body: The researchers say childlessness is increasingly concentrated among people with fewer resources. A fertility researcher at Aarhus University pointed to finances as a likely factor; the researchers also cited housing conditions and rising expectations about what parents should provide. The report says the pattern is not expected to create a problem for the national economy, but may affect individuals who want children.

content.headline: U2’s new album finds the band sounding joyful and newly sure of itself
content.shortHeadline: U2 sound renewed on Carnaval de Luz
content.standfirst: Their first album of new songs in almost nine years arrives after a turbulent stretch. A review hears a band rekindling its classic sound, while an interview traces the hard-won democracy that has kept its four members together.

image.caption: The Edge with Bono, Larry Mullen and Adam Clayton.

sources.originalTitle: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump

segments.body: With drummer Larry Mullen Jr back after medical issues, U2 sound newly energised on Carnaval de Luz, their first album of new songs in almost nine years. The review finds their familiar loud guitars, spiritual imagery and earnest uplift working again, even if not every track reaches the same heights.

segments.title: A band built to last
segments.body: In a conversation marking 50 years since the group formed, U2 describe songwriting credits shared equally and decisions made by committee as their “soviet”. The arrangement has sometimes tested the band, they say, but the Edge argues that U2 would be a different group without any one of its four members.

perspectives.body: The interview adds the band’s own account of survival: its members see shared credit and collective decision-making not as a theory but as the structure that has kept them together for five decades.

content.headline: Jorge Drexler turned a life in medicine into songs that make people dance
content.shortHeadline: Jorge Drexler finds freedom in dance
content.standfirst: The Uruguayan doctor-turned-songwriter says the effects of growing up under dictatorship took decades to leave his body. His new album returns to candombe, the music of home, as it earns eight Latin Grammy nominations.

image.caption: Musicians and participants perform in a candombe session in Montevideo.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner

segments.body: Jorge Drexler says he did not dance until he was 45. Raised in Montevideo under a dictatorship hostile to artists, he began making music while studying medicine and working as an ear, nose and throat specialist. Now 62, he has built a songwriting career that brings scientific ideas and poetry together.

segments.title: A return to candombe
segments.body: His latest album, Taracá, is a return to the candombe sound of Uruguay and follows the death of his father. It brings together Latin American musicians including guitarist Julio Cobelli and rapper Young Miko. The record is nominated for eight Latin Grammys, due to be presented on 12 November.

content.headline: Television guitarist Richard Lloyd, a force in 1970s punk, dies at 75
content.shortHeadline: Television guitarist Richard Lloyd dies at 75
content.standfirst: Lloyd’s family says he died at home in Tennessee from bile duct cancer. As a founding member of Television, he helped shape the New York punk scene around CBGB and played on the influential album Marquee Moon.

image.caption: Richard Lloyd performing in Minneapolis in 2009.

sources.originalTitle: Richard Lloyd, founding member and guitarist of punk band Television, dies aged 75

segments.body: Richard Lloyd, founding guitarist of Television, has died aged 75, his family says. He died at home in Chattanooga, Tennessee, on Saturday morning. His family said he had been diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer, in March 2026.

segments.title: A landmark guitar sound
segments.body: Television formed in 1973 and became one of the earliest punk groups to play at CBGB in New York. The band recorded two studio albums at the height of its late-1970s run; its debut, Marquee Moon, is now widely regarded as a landmark guitar record.

content.headline: At 93, Willie Nelson says he never expected to survive his hard years
content.shortHeadline: Willie Nelson on survival, loss and the road
content.standfirst: The country legend discusses his memoir, cannabis, touring and the friends he has outlived. An excerpt from the book adds his own reflections on grief, family and the habits that helped him keep making music.

image.caption: Willie Nelson.

sources.originalTitle: Willie Nelson: ‘I drank too much, I smoked too much. I took too many pills’
Stay sharp, get used to loss – and pay your taxes: the wit and wisdom of Willie Nelson

segments.body: Willie Nelson, 93, says he did not expect to live this long: “I did everything wrong.” He describes giving up alcohol after years of heavy drinking and pills, and stopping smoking cannabis at 86 after lung problems. He still uses cannabis in food and drink and says performing continues to make him feel good.

segments.title: A life turned into songs
segments.body: In an extract from his memoir, Nelson writes that grief does not disappear, but can be turned into a song. He recalls the friends who helped him through financial trouble, his family life on the road and the importance of listening. The book’s reflections complement the interview’s account of ageing and survival.

perspectives.body: The memoir excerpt offers Nelson’s own first-person perspective on loss and resilience: songwriting, he writes, has been his way of making heavy thoughts lighter, rather than pretending they can be left behind.

content.headline: Skepta’s The Fork and Knife turns grime history into a story of legacy
content.shortHeadline: Skepta looks back and moves forward on The Fork and Knife
content.standfirst: After seven years between albums, the grime pioneer moves from familiar rhythms into a portrait of a life and a wider Black British musical history. The review finds the record most compelling when Skepta makes room for the artists coming after him.

sources.originalTitle: The Fork and Knife

segments.body: Skepta’s first album in seven years takes time to find its shape, the review says, opening with some familiar grime and rap sounds. As the record unfolds, those early echoes become part of a broader look at a career spanning three decades and the many strands of Black British music.

segments.title: A wider inheritance
segments.body: The album draws together Skepta’s family history, grime, fashion, dance music and newer collaborators. On its nine-minute “Belly” cypher, the review hears the veteran MC sharing the spotlight with younger voices; elsewhere, the record presents immigrant Britain as a story of achievement and possibility.

content.headline: Kings of Leon reinvent themselves with the warm country-rock of O My Beloved
content.shortHeadline: Kings of Leon loosen up on O My Beloved
content.standfirst: The band’s tenth album turns away from the arena-rock sound that defined its biggest hits. The review hears a more spacious, country-leaning group, even as traces of its old bombast sometimes return.

sources.originalTitle: O My Beloved

segments.body: O My Beloved is a striking shift for Kings of Leon, whose recent records often leaned into a large, polished arena sound. Here the band favour warmer, more spacious country-rock, with acoustic-led songs that give the group a looser feel than it has had in years.

segments.title: Old habits remain
segments.body: The review finds the reinvention most persuasive in its quieter songs, while some bigger choruses recall the band’s late-2000s sound. The record is not without weaker moments, but its new maturity makes the group newly worth watching.

content.headline: Dream Unending’s Certain Uncertainties drifts from doom metal into cowboy jazz
content.shortHeadline: Dream Unending loosen the grip of metal
content.standfirst: The duo’s third album increasingly favours open-ended psychedelia and quieter textures over heaviness. The review admires the boldest departures, while finding the shifts less convincing when the record tries to reconcile them with doom metal.

sources.originalTitle: Certain Uncertainties

segments.body: Dream Unending continue to move away from the heaviness that shaped their earlier work. Certain Uncertainties includes long stretches with little connection to metal, drawing instead on cosmic country, spiritual jazz and open-ended psychedelia. The review calls it a striking, if sometimes uneasy, change of direction.

segments.title: Where the experiment works
segments.body: The instrumental title track and “I Carry Your Burden” are singled out for their calm, spacious sound. The review is less convinced when the record returns to heavier material, where the different styles can feel divided rather than fully fused.

content.headline: Aphex Twin’s once-divisive Drukqs now looks central to his musical legacy
content.shortHeadline: Why Aphex Twin’s Drukqs still matters
content.standfirst: A quarter-century on, the sprawling album’s collision of rave rhythms, prepared piano and digital precision feels less like a detour than a key to Richard D. James’s work. A close listen finds its tensions between dancefloor and concert hall still alive.

sources.originalTitle: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: When Drukqs appeared in 2001, its length and wild shifts in style made it difficult to place. The anniversary review hears a work that brings together the two histories of electronic music: club rhythms and the more formal experiments of the concert hall.

segments.title: The beat at the edge of rhythm
segments.body: Across the album, Richard D. James pushes percussion toward the point where rhythm becomes pitch, then sets tightly programmed piano against volatile electronic beats. The review argues that the apparent disorder is central to Drukqs: its music strains against boundaries between acoustic and electronic, human and machine, and dance music and experimental composition.

content.headline: 1 in 2 turns a filmmaker’s bowel cancer treatment into a plea to act sooner
content.shortHeadline: 1 in 2 asks why bowel cancer affects younger people
content.standfirst: David Wilkinson films his own treatment and meets people in their 20s, 30s and 40s facing the disease. His documentary asks why cases are rising among younger people and urges viewers not to delay getting tested.

image.caption: David Wilkinson in 1 in 2.

sources.originalTitle: 1 in 2 review – compassionate film about dealing with bowel cancer is a personal plea on behalf of the young

segments.body: Filmmaker David Wilkinson was being treated for stage four bowel cancer while making his previous film. In 1 in 2, he turns the camera on himself and on younger people he meets through cancer support groups, asking why a disease associated with older people is increasingly affecting people in their 20s, 30s and 40s.

segments.title: Questions without clear answers
segments.body: The film speaks with patients and NHS professionals, but finds no settled explanation for the rise. Diet and lifestyle may be factors; the possibility of microplastics is raised, not resolved. The review praises the documentary’s compassion and supports its practical message: take the bowel cancer test and do not put it off.

content.headline: A Fox Under a Pink Moon turns one teenager’s refugee journey into art
content.shortHeadline: A Fox Under a Pink Moon: a refugee’s filmed journey
content.standfirst: Soraya Akhlaghi recorded five years of flight, danger and precarious life on her phone. The resulting documentary combines that footage with animation inspired by her drawings, giving imaginative form to an experience marked by repeated uncertainty.

image.caption: Soraya Akhlaghi in A Fox Under a Pink Moon.

sources.originalTitle: A Fox Under a Pink Moon review – Iranian teen refugee paints boldly imaginative self-portrait

segments.body: Soraya Akhlaghi was 16 when she began filming her attempts to flee Iran and reach her mother in Austria. Over five years, her journey took her through asylum centres, border crossings and back to Tehran, where she lived with a violent husband. Co-director Mehrdad Oskouei assembled her phone footage remotely.

segments.title: Drawing a way through
segments.body: Akhlaghi’s drawings give the film a second language: a moon, a fox, a clown-like version of herself and figures representing her fears recur in animated sequences. The review sees this art as a source of imaginative space and resilience amid a life that repeatedly returns her to danger.

content.headline: Why Gone Girl is one writer’s dark, oddly comforting annual rewatch
content.shortHeadline: The dark comfort of Gone Girl
content.standfirst: David Fincher’s thriller is an unconventional comfort film, its writer argues: a story of marital collapse in which Rosamund Pike’s Amy turns the assumptions made about her into a weapon. The pleasure is unsettling, but that is part of the appeal.

image.caption: Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Sadistic, forbidden pleasure’: why Gone Girl is my feelgood movie

segments.body: Gone Girl may seem an unlikely comfort watch: Amy Dunne disappears, her husband becomes a suspect, and the marriage at the centre of the story is full of resentment and infidelity. But this writer returns to David Fincher’s 2014 thriller each year, drawn to its carefully built tension and Amy’s revenge.

segments.title: A performance of expectation
segments.body: As the mystery turns, Amy understands how the public is likely to see a missing wife and a cheating husband—and uses those expectations to her advantage. The essay connects the film’s appeal to its sharp portrait of the “cool girl” ideal and the freedom of watching Amy refuse to be made small.

content.headline: 100 Sunset drifts through a Toronto Tibetan community in a dreamlike debut
content.shortHeadline: 100 Sunset: a quiet, elusive Toronto drama
content.standfirst: Kunsang Kyirong’s first feature follows an introverted young woman whose theft of a camcorder draws her into the lives of her neighbours. Its restrained, uncertain storytelling reflects the disorientation of its characters.

image.caption: Sonam Choekyi in 100 Sunset.

sources.originalTitle: 100 Sunset review – elliptical, elusive drama dreamlike through Toronto’s tight-knit Tibetan community

segments.body: In Kunsang Kyirong’s debut feature, 18-year-old Kunsel lives in a Toronto apartment block shared by a close-knit Tibetan community. After stealing a camcorder, she begins filming her neighbours, especially Passang, a young woman who has recently moved into the building.

segments.title: A story that refuses to settle
segments.body: Kunsel and Passang become friends, while a missing suitcase of money hints at a more conventional suspense plot. The film lets that thread recede, the review says, favouring a drifting mood that mirrors Kunsel’s inwardness and the community’s sense of displacement.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson’s reported place in the Bond race makes the casting interesting
content.shortHeadline: Could Robert Pattinson make Bond strange again?
content.standfirst: Reports say Pattinson is among the actors considered for 007. The prospect is intriguing not because his casting is confirmed—it is not—but because his appetite for odd, unpredictable roles could unsettle the franchise’s familiar shape.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson.

sources.originalTitle: Robert Pattinson has auditioned for James Bond – and finally the 007 race is interesting

segments.body: Reports from Hollywood trade publications place Robert Pattinson among the contenders for the next James Bond, alongside actors including Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner and Nicholas Hoult. The next 007 has not been cast, but the possibility has prompted a fresh look at what Pattinson might bring to the role.

segments.title: An unpredictable leading man
segments.body: The column argues that Pattinson’s habit of seeking out strange and varied characters could make him an unusually compelling Bond—if he were offered the part and given room to reshape it. Those are both open questions: his candidacy is reported, not confirmed, and the franchise’s handlers may prefer a more conventional approach.

content.headline: Bluey producer Daley Pearson’s film Allen turns childhood nostalgia into a story
content.shortHeadline: Daley Pearson on the childhood grief behind Allen
content.standfirst: The Ludo Studio co-founder says his new Netflix family film grew from the loss of his brother and his own attachment to childhood pop culture. Its funny story of a boy and an alien also asks what happens when nostalgia keeps an adult from moving forward.

image.caption: Allen and Daley Pearson.

sources.originalTitle: Bluey’s Daley Pearson on how losing his brother inspired his new film: ‘He was the best thing ever to me’

segments.body: Allen follows Petey, who befriends an alien as a child and struggles to move on after it leaves. Decades later, the alien returns. Director and co-writer Daley Pearson says the story draws on his own attachment to childhood memories and the fear of being held back by them.

segments.title: A loss behind the comedy
segments.body: Pearson says the story is also connected to his older brother Liam, who died of cancer when Pearson was 13. He describes the film as an attempt to understand the longing to recover something precious—and how that longing can leave a person waiting rather than living. He also wants it to work as a silly, enjoyable family adventure.

content.headline: Ava DuVernay’s 14th examines the fight over birthright citizenship
content.shortHeadline: Ava DuVernay turns to the 14th Amendment
content.standfirst: A decade after 13th, DuVernay’s new documentary explores the US constitutional amendment at the heart of a new battle over citizenship and rights. She says making the film helped her process fear and anger at what she sees happening around her.

image.caption: Ava DuVernay.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve seen people in my neighbourhood pulled out of their cars’: Ava DuVernay on the cruelty and brutality of Trump’s America

segments.body: Ava DuVernay began making 14th after President Trump’s 2025 executive order challenging birthright citizenship. As she researched the amendment’s five sections, she says, she came to see attacks on more than citizenship and built the film around the wider struggle over its protections.

segments.title: A broad argument, and an open question
segments.body: The documentary brings together 50 interviews, from historians and constitutional experts to political figures and a livestreamer, to present a range of ideological and generational views. DuVernay also discusses using animation and AI to move real archival photographs, while acknowledging wider concern about the technology.

content.headline: La Bola Negra links three Spanish lives through queer history and desire
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra finds poetry in Spain’s queer past
content.standfirst: This three-part drama moves between 1932, 1939 and 2017 to tell stories of gay men living under different forms of pressure. The review praises its performances and visual confidence, while noting that explaining its connections can diminish some of its mystery.

image.caption: Álvaro Lafuente Calvo in La Bola Negra.

sources.originalTitle: La Bola Negra review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly told

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows three men in different eras of Spanish life: Carlos, rejected by an elite club amid rumours about his sexuality; Sebastián, conscripted into Franco’s army and drawn to a Republican prisoner; and Alberto, a researcher whose inheritance unsettles his family. The film takes its title and inspiration from Federico García Lorca.

segments.title: History, memory and mystery
segments.body: The review praises the film’s performances, detailed production and the way it connects private lives to Spain’s political history. It also finds that spelling out the links between the three strands costs the story some of the mystery that makes its treatment of queer memory so affecting.

content.headline: Naturewatch brings Chris Packham’s wildlife answers to a weekly video show
content.shortHeadline: Chris Packham answers wildlife questions in Naturewatch
content.standfirst: Packham, Kyle Thomas and Megan McCubbin take on questions such as “What are wasps for?” in a new weekly video podcast, with guest experts and a promise of “guaranteed nerdiness”. The show is also due to air on BBC Two.

image.caption: Kyle Thomas, Chris Packham and Megan McCubbin present Naturewatch.

sources.originalTitle: Chris Packham’s lovely new wildlife show: best podcasts of the week

segments.body: Naturewatch is a weekly wildlife video podcast hosted by Chris Packham, Kyle Thomas and Megan McCubbin. The team answers viewers’ questions, from whether bats are really blind to what wasps contribute, with guest experts joining from a countryside base near Bristol.

The Guardian’s weekly podcast guide describes the programme as an inviting option for viewers who enjoy getting into the detail of nature. It is also scheduled to stream on Fridays at 7.30pm on BBC Two.

content.headline: The week’s TV picks include Rivals, a Zurich heist and a return to City of God
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: This week’s guide ranges from Rivals’ mix of grief and scandal to a multi-timeline bank-heist thriller and a second season of City of God. It also points viewers towards new fantasy, true crime and a Peanuts Christmas special.

sources.originalTitle: Rivals to 12 12 12: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Rivals returns to its world of romantic entanglements and workplace conflict after Monica’s death, while a new thriller, 12 12 12, tracks a Zurich bank robbery across a year of planning, 12 hours of action and 12 days of police work. The guide finds the latter’s plot inventive, though its characters could be more fully drawn.

segments.title: Crime and fantasy
segments.body: A second season of City of God brings a photojournalist back to the favela, where gangsters begin to consider politics as well as violence. The guide also highlights the return of The Rings of Power and two true-crime series, one focused on a murder investigation and the other on retired Hungarian detectives reflecting on police work during a transition from autocracy to democracy.
For something lighter, a new Peanuts animation gives Snoopy a Christmas-list dilemma. The guide recommends it for hitting its familiar, wholesome notes with charm and precision.

content.headline: Mums v Big Pharma follows two mothers’ campaign over sodium valproate
content.shortHeadline: Two mothers take on Big Pharma in Mums v Big Pharma
content.standfirst: This documentary revisits the harm caused to generations of children by sodium valproate and the campaign for accountability. At its centre are Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, whose persistence is set against official delay and resistance.

image.caption: Janet Williams and Emma Murphy in Mums v Big Pharma.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: a stirring documentary about two mothers taking on Big Pharma

segments.body: Mums v Big Pharma examines the continuing campaign over sodium valproate, an epilepsy drug prescribed despite concerns emerging during testing. The documentary follows Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, two mothers who have pushed for answers in the face of official inertia and, at times, open scorn.

content.headline: Rise of the Rockstar Chef serves up the Ramsay–Marco Pierre White feud
content.shortHeadline: Ramsay and White’s kitchen feud takes centre stage
content.standfirst: The docuseries treats the rise of British fine dining like a band story, with Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White revisiting their bitter break. The review finds the rivalry gripping, if the third participant, Heston Blumenthal, is often left in the background.

image.caption: Heston Blumenthal, Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White in Rise of the Rockstar Chef.

sources.originalTitle: Rise of the Rockstar Chef review – Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White serve up the most sizzling TV of the year

segments.body: Rise of the Rockstar Chef revisits how Gordon Ramsay, Marco Pierre White and Heston Blumenthal helped transform Britain’s restaurant scene. The series turns chefs’ careers into a music-style origin story, complete with arguments about stolen reservations, restaurant rivalries and an eventual reunion between Ramsay and his former mentor.

segments.title: A rivalry that still simmers
segments.body: The review says the series is at its liveliest when Ramsay and White recount their conflicting versions of the feud. It also notes that the production gives White much of the spotlight and leaves Blumenthal feeling like a supporting player, while giving a revealing account of the toxic kitchen culture around the chefs’ success.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale finds a last-minute victory for the Faithful
content.shortHeadline: A late twist saves The Celebrity Traitors finale
content.standfirst: After a series the reviewer found flat, Sebastian’s late suspicion of Kenny changes the ending. The Faithful win £83,000 for charity, while the finale’s account of Maya’s careful deception and the players’ shifting egos gives the game a final jolt.

image.caption: The Endgame Round Table in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The Celebrity Traitors seemed headed for a win by Kenny, with most of the Faithful missing the evidence around them. After Maya is banished, Kenny chooses to end the game; Sebastian realises that a Traitor would have reason to do so, and persuades Romesh Ranganathan to change his vote. The Faithful win £83,000 for charity.

segments.title: The value of staying out of the spotlight
segments.body: The review argues that Sebastian’s lack of ego helped him notice what others missed. It contrasts his last-minute intervention with Maya’s confidence and Michael Sheen’s influential accusations, which had made him a target. After a series the writer found predictable, the reversal made the finale feel newly exciting.

content.headline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife’s pause, ageing and caring for her mother
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on life between Call the Midwife series
content.standfirst: With Call the Midwife taking a break, Main is touring in a play about Elizabeth II and helping care for her mother in Aberdeen. She reflects on the long-running role, the value of letting Shelagh age naturally and the pressures faced by unpaid carers.

image.caption: Laura Main in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Laura Main has played Shelagh on Call the Midwife since its 2012 debut, but has not filmed the show this year as it takes a sabbatical. The BBC has confirmed a sixteenth series and a film, though Main says no dates have been set. A Christmas prequel, Sisters in Arms, is planned instead.

segments.title: Work, care and ageing
segments.body: Main is touring in By Royal Appointment while helping care for her 91-year-old mother. She says the experience has made her think about the support carers need, and about the choice to let Shelagh age at the same rate as the actor playing her—even when she might personally prefer to slow the passage of time.

content.headline: A Matthew Perry documentary revisits his addiction but leaves hard questions
content.shortHeadline: The Matthew Perry documentary: moving, but intrusive
content.standfirst: Netflix’s three-part series draws on family testimony and archive footage to revisit the Friends actor’s addiction and death. The review finds it moving at times, but questions the value of asking loved ones to relive their loss without uncovering more about what happened.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry follows the actor from his rise to fame on Friends to his work as an addiction campaigner and his death in 2023. Family members describe the generous friend they knew as well as the isolation and addiction that shaped much of his life. Much of the story, the review notes, was already told in Perry’s 2022 memoir.

segments.title: What the series leaves unexplored
segments.body: The review finds the documentary’s treatment of Perry’s death cursory, despite testimony about the ketamine he was using and the people who supplied it. It also questions the decision to linger on relatives recounting the moment they learned he had died, arguing that their distress adds little insight.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into the world of divorce law
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new family
content.standfirst: The BBC spin-off moves from London to Manchester and centres a predominantly British Asian family and law firm. Its creators say it keeps the original’s mix of relationships and legal drama while making everyday British Asian lives its subject.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expected to take over her family’s divorce-law firm, until her mother’s death changes her father’s succession plans. The six-part BBC drama moves the action to Manchester and gives the legal-family story a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team.

segments.title: Representation as ordinary life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than relying on familiar storylines about terrorism or arranged marriage. Original series creator Abi Morgan, now an executive producer, says the spin-off keeps the focus on family and relationships while supporting a new team of writers and performers.

perspectives.body: Sarma’s emphasis is not only on who appears on screen: she describes the aim as portraying a specific family truthfully, without trying to represent every facet of British Asian life through a single set of characters.

content.headline: How Grand Theft Auto grew from a crime game into a cultural colossus
content.shortHeadline: Grand Theft Auto’s life beyond the crime spree
content.standfirst: As GTA VI approaches, a feature traces the series’ changing worlds, from its early open-city experiments to the dense simulations of modern Los Santos. Its appeal, the reporting argues, lies as much in drifting through those worlds as in breaking their rules.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

segments.body: The first Grand Theft Auto, made by Scotland’s DMA Design in 1997, offered a playful view of crime in fictional US cities. Later games built detailed open worlds shaped by film, music and literature, while moving beyond those influences into a distinct form of city-making.

segments.title: The world between missions
segments.body: The feature argues that GTA’s power is not simply its criminal fantasy. Players also remember the stretches between missions: driving aimlessly, exploring or watching the sun move across a landscape. Rockstar’s film influences—from Scarface and Miami Vice to Boyz n the Hood and Heat—helped define the series, but the games’ open worlds have become the point in themselves.

perspectives.body: A game critic interviewed for the feature describes GTA’s world as something players can inhabit rather than merely pass through: its incidental details and unhurried moments, not only its missions, create the sense of being inside a place.

segments.title: A world of contradictions
segments.body: GTA is both a satire of consumerism and a hugely profitable franchise, and a game about criminals made by a studio based in Edinburgh while depicting an American landscape. The feature suggests these tensions help explain why the series remains compelling—and why its simulated world feels so inviting in an age of artificial digital content.

content.headline: The Ocarina of Time remake makes a landmark Zelda feel new again
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time becomes a modern Zelda masterpiece
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s ambitious remake keeps the original’s journeys and puzzles but adds voiced scenes, richer visuals and easier controls. The review finds that the updates deepen the story without losing its melancholy.

image.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

segments.body: The remake preserves Ocarina of Time’s familiar journey through Hyrule and its puzzle-filled temples. What changes is the presentation: expanded dialogue and fully voiced scenes bring more drama to a story that had to be told with restraint on the Nintendo 64.

segments.title: A story about time
segments.body: More flexible movement, quicker access to equipment and an orchestral score make the game easier to play and more vivid. The review also notes an alteration it dislikes—the warrior Sheik has lost some of the original’s androgyny—but finds that the remake retains the story’s central sadness: a child’s years are stolen as he is drawn into saving the world.

content.headline: A Zelda midnight launch brings fans together—and tests their patience
content.shortHeadline: The Zelda midnight launch was a long night for fans
content.standfirst: Hundreds queued on London’s Oxford Street for the Ocarina of Time remake and its limited-edition keepsakes. The writer’s four-hour wait began as a celebration of shared fandom and ended with many still waiting to be sent their collectible box.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

segments.body: About 500 fans gathered outside an Argos on Oxford Street for the midnight release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. In an age when most games are downloaded, the launch offered a rare chance to meet fellow fans and collect a special box and ocarina-shaped keyring.

segments.title: The wait outlasts the excitement
segments.body: The writer queued for four hours before the store closed, with some customers asked to leave their details so the promised box could be posted later. The event began as a reminder of the pleasure of gaming as a shared ritual; the long wait and uncertainty about the collectables eventually wore down that feeling.

content.headline: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring film faces the challenge of making its world matter
content.shortHeadline: Can the Elden Ring film make its world matter?
content.standfirst: The game’s vast, horrific fantasy setting and a reported budget near $200m raise the stakes for its film adaptation. The central challenge, the feature argues, is not merely showing the world but giving viewers a reason to care about spending time in it.

image.caption: Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s adaptation of Elden Ring has reportedly been shot and is in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Jonathan Pryce. The game has sold more than 30 million copies, and the reported budget is close to $200m, making this a high-stakes attempt to bring its fantasy world to film.

segments.title: A world without easy answers
segments.body: The game’s horror-tinged landscapes and sparse, hostile world differ sharply from the reassurance of familiar fantasy adventures. The feature asks whether the film can turn that scale and strangeness into a compelling story, while noting that Garland’s previous films have resisted conventional happy endings. How much freedom he will have on a project of this size remains unknown.

content.headline: Replaying Call of Duty with his son turns a difficult mission into family time
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reunite through an old Call of Duty
content.standfirst: A father and his 22-year-old son revisit the co-op missions they first played when the son was five. Their renewed teamwork turns repeated failures into a moving account of how games can preserve a relationship across time.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game father and son play together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his adult son return to the Special Ops missions in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, a game they first played together in 2009. At first their styles clash: one moves cautiously, while the other rushes ahead. They fail repeatedly, but gradually learn to work together and complete missions they never finished when the son was five.

segments.title: A bond with a deadline
segments.body: The father says the weeks of shared gaming have given him a break from adult responsibilities and a chance to feel carefree again. He and his son expect to move to different parts of the world in a few months; the son tells him he will remember this time as some of their best together.

content.headline: Stonehenge altar stone did not come from north-east Scotland, study suggests
content.shortHeadline: Stonehenge altar stone: Scotland theory ruled out
content.standfirst: New tests make a north-east Scotland origin for Stonehenge’s six-tonne altar stone very unlikely. Researchers have narrowed the search, but say its source could still lie elsewhere in Scotland, northern England or Ireland.

image.caption: Stonehenge’s altar stone lies beneath two sarsen stones in Wiltshire, England.

sources.originalTitle: Origin of Stonehenge’s altar remains enigma as north-east Scotland theory ruled out

segments.body: A new geological investigation has found it is “very unlikely” that Stonehenge’s altar stone came from north-east Scotland, challenging a theory proposed in 2024. Researchers tested samples from the stone and compared them with rock collected in the region, but have not yet identified where it originated.

segments.title: The search continues
segments.body: The study’s leader, Duncan Pirrie, said the stone definitely did not come from southern Britain, while other possible origins include elsewhere in Scotland, northern England or Ireland. The researchers say ruling out locations is part of narrowing the search; none examined so far matches the stone’s full profile.

content.headline: Tiny medical robots show promise in tests, but human use is still years away
content.shortHeadline: Medical micro-robots: promise in early tests
content.standfirst: Researchers are developing magnetically steered devices to deliver drugs inside the body. Tests in pigs and mice are promising, but the smallest robots remain experimental and devices for use in patients are likely years away.

image.caption: Illustration of a miniature medical robot designed to deliver drugs in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: Miniature medical robots are being developed to deliver drugs to precise sites, investigate the gut and potentially treat conditions such as tumours or blood clots. One research team in Beijing reported using a 6.5mm device to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs; this was an animal test, not a treatment demonstrated in people.

segments.title: From gut to bloodstream
segments.body: Other early-stage work includes a 2mm robot guided through a pig’s bloodstream and magnetic particles that heated and destroyed tumours in mice. Researchers say precise delivery could reduce the amount of a drug needed, but devices small enough to travel through human blood vessels are still some way from clinical use.

content.headline: Bird flu in Utah mink raises concern about mutation and pandemic risk
content.shortHeadline: Bird flu in mink: why researchers are concerned
content.standfirst: An outbreak on a Utah fur farm has heightened concern because mink may host both bird and human flu viruses. Experts warn that a change in the virus is possible, not inevitable, and say preparedness includes better tests and surveillance.

image.caption: Mink on fur farms may provide conditions in which a new flu strain could emerge.

sources.originalTitle: Bird flu is one mutation from serious risk to humans – how prepared is the UK?

segments.body: Bird flu has been spreading among mink on a Utah farm since at least August, according to the report. Scientists are concerned because mink are mammals with respiratory systems considered similar to humans, and could potentially host both bird and human flu strains. That creates a possibility of the viruses exchanging genetic material, but there is no report here of human-to-human spread from this outbreak.

segments.title: Preparedness questions
segments.body: The UK Health Security Agency said it has systems to detect human cases and is ready to respond. Researchers cited in the report say seasonal flu vaccination would be unlikely to protect people fully against a new pandemic strain; they also call for testing whether existing flu kits detect bird flu and for a practical exercise to develop suitable tests quickly.

content.headline: Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives could leave some short of iodine
content.shortHeadline: Plant-based swaps may reduce iodine intake
content.standfirst: A UK dietary analysis suggests replacing dairy with unfortified plant alternatives could increase iodine deficiency, particularly among teenagers. The findings model potential dietary changes; they do not show that every plant-based drink lacks nutrients.

image.caption: People in the UK are increasingly turning to non-dairy milk.

sources.originalTitle: Tired and putting on weight? This could be the surprising reason

segments.body: A study combining UK dietary data with manufacturers’ nutrition information estimated that replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives could lower iodine intake. The modelling found that if teenagers replaced half their dairy products, 80% of girls and 72% of boys could be deficient; the researchers say teenage girls are already the group most likely to fall short.

segments.title: Fortification matters
segments.body: The risk depends on what products people choose: only one in 10 plant-based alternatives in the analysis was fortified with iodine. The Vegan Society recommends choosing fortified alternatives, and the study found that standardised iodine fortification of substitutes and bread could help avoid deficiency even if people switched entirely from dairy.

content.headline: Nvidia launches independent probe into CEO’s relationship with alleged Chinese…
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia probes CEO’s relationship amid espionage allegations
content.standfirst: Nvidia says independent directors and outside counsel will investigate reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, whom US officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. The company says it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised; China rejects the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”

segments.body: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation after reporting linked CEO Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data-centre company Megaspeed. Jensen Huang acknowledged in a memo to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. US officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, but the reporting does not establish that she obtained or passed on information.

segments.title: What the probe must establish
segments.body: Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe that company secrets or US national security were compromised and says Huang supports the inquiry. China has called the spying allegations groundless. The BBC reports that it remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang allegedly gathered; Nvidia and Megaspeed’s roles in any transfer of information remain unresolved.

segments.title: An unusually high-stakes board decision
segments.body: Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, speaking to TechCrunch, put the odds of Huang keeping his job at “about a 50-50” and highlighted Nvidia’s central role in the AI economy and the lack of an obvious successor. That is an outside expert’s assessment, not a company decision or a finding of the investigation.

perspectives.body: Sonnenfeld’s analysis focuses on the consequences of a leadership crisis at a company that supplies chips and has financial ties across the AI industry. He also says the board will need to establish whether any technology reached China and by what route.

content.headline: US regulators reopen Waymo school-bus safety case after reports persisted
content.shortHeadline: US probes Waymo school-bus incidents after software fix
content.standfirst: The US road-safety regulator says most reported cases of Waymo robotaxis passing stopped school buses occurred after a software update intended to fix the behaviour. Its new review will assess whether the remedy was adequate.

sources.originalTitle: Waymo robotaxis kept illegally passing school buses after software fix, feds say

segments.body: The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened a recall query into Waymo after reports that its robotaxis continued to pass stopped school buses with flashing lights after a software update. The regulator says a majority of the incidents it reviewed happened after the fix was deployed, and is assessing whether the remedy was adequate.

segments.title: Incidents under review
segments.body: The agency had first opened an investigation in October 2025 after video showed a Waymo vehicle manoeuvring around a stopped bus unloading children in Atlanta. School officials in Austin later reported at least five incidents. Waymo had not responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment by the article’s publication.

content.headline: UK may cut electric-car sales target, but government says no decision made
content.shortHeadline: UK EV target cut reportedly under consideration
content.standfirst: The Guardian reports ministers are expected to reduce the 2030 electric-car sales target, with a cut to about 60% among the options. The government says no decision has been taken and maintains its longer-term zero-emission commitments.

image.caption: Carmakers have warned that interim electric-vehicle sales targets are difficult to meet.

sources.originalTitle: Labour expected to cut EV targets for UK’s car industry despite MPs’ protests

segments.body: Ministers are expected to weaken the UK’s zero-emission vehicle mandate, with government sources telling the Guardian that the 2030 target could fall from 80% to about 60%, alongside an extension of compliance flexibilities. The government says no decision has been taken and says its commitment to end sales of new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel by 2030 remains in place.

segments.title: Industry and climate stakes
segments.body: Carmakers say sales are falling short of current interim targets: battery-electric vehicles made up 26.6% of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders. Critics of a reduction warn it could undermine emissions plans and investment in charging infrastructure; the final policy remains unconfirmed.

content.headline: AI-generated complaints are adding to workloads across UK public services
content.shortHeadline: UK public services face a flood of AI-drafted complaints
content.standfirst: Public bodies, MPs’ offices and employers say chatbot-written complaints and requests are longer and more demanding to process. AI can help people make their case, but officials warn that inaccurate or irrelevant material is consuming scarce staff time.

image.caption: AI-generated correspondence can take little time to write but much longer for staff to process.

sources.originalTitle: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints

segments.body: UK public bodies and other organisations report rising volumes of correspondence drafted with generative AI, from complaints and freedom-of-information requests to legal challenges. Staff say the messages can be much longer and harder to assess than earlier submissions, even when the tools help people put their concerns into formal language.

segments.title: The cost of volume
segments.body: The Information Commissioner’s Office says AI-written requests can be repetitive, inaccurate or difficult to interpret, but still need a human response. The Guardian reports that some local-authority complaints have grown from about two pages on average to far longer; one caseworker described a 200-page submission. Public bodies are considering summaries and templates, amid concerns that filtering AI with AI could bring costs and lose the human touch.

content.headline: Meta expands Instagram’s AI system for placing suspected teens in protected…
content.shortHeadline: Meta expands Instagram’s AI teen-account system
content.standfirst: Meta says it is expanding globally a system that estimates whether Instagram users are teenagers and can place them in more restrictive Teen Account settings, even if they gave an adult birthday. The company says the safeguards include private-by-default accounts and limits on direct messages.

sources.originalTitle: Instagram’s AI age detection is expanding globally
Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally

segments.body: Meta is expanding Instagram’s AI-powered age-estimation system worldwide. It looks for signals that a user may be 13 to 17 and can move the account into Teen Account protections even if the person entered an adult birth date. Meta says the settings make accounts private by default, limit some content and restrict messages from strangers.

segments.title: What the system does—and does not do
segments.body: Meta says it uses clues across profiles, including posts and biographical details, and announced the expansion amid legal scrutiny over protections for young users. The Verge’s report clarifies that this expansion concerns teen settings; identifying and removing users under 13 is a separate process. The system estimates age—it is not described as a definitive age check.

content.headline: Google plans to place ads in AI Mode follow-up answers and expand to more…
content.shortHeadline: Google brings ads into AI Mode follow-up answers
content.standfirst: Google says sponsored listings will appear in some US follow-up answers in AI Mode and is expanding AI ads to more countries. The move could give advertisers more space in conversational search while intensifying pressure on publishers seeking visits from Google.

image.caption: Google plans to expand ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode.

sources.originalTitle: Google’s AI Mode Will Soon Show Ads Even in Your Follow-Up Questions

segments.body: Google plans to show what it calls “multiturn ads” within some AI Mode follow-up answers in the US, when a conversation has commercial relevance. It is also expanding advertising in AI Mode to 10 more countries, with launches in Brazil, Mexico and the UK planned later this year, according to CNET.

segments.title: Competition for attention
segments.body: Google says sponsored product listings in AI Mode are clicked about as often as organic results. SEO specialist Lily Ray, quoted by CNET, warns that ads and AI answers could make it harder for users to find publishers’ articles through search. The extent of any further traffic decline is not established by the announcement itself.

content.headline: Medium’s TK app mixes AI writing help with private group publishing
content.shortHeadline: Medium’s TK app pairs AI writing tools with private publishing
content.standfirst: Medium’s new TK app combines note-taking, AI assistance and small-group sharing. Its launch also sharpens a debate over whether AI can support writers without taking over their work—and how readers should be told when it has been used.

image.caption: Medium’s TK writing app combines notes, AI assistance and sharing.

sources.originalTitle: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK

segments.body: Medium has launched TK, a writing app that can help users organise notes, get editorial feedback and fill in information while drafting. It also lets users share early work in private groups. The app is free for people with a Medium account, and Medium says authors can publish notes explaining how they used AI.

segments.title: Where assistance ends
segments.body: TechCrunch describes concerns that AI suggestions could become the writing itself, as well as limits in AI-detection tools. Medium says TK is designed to make the provenance of writing transparent; the app’s support for prompting and source material is a stated aim, not independent evidence that its tools can reliably establish how a text was produced.

content.headline: Music industry body warns Australia against weakening copyright rules for AI
content.shortHeadline: Music industry warns Australia over AI copyright proposals
content.standfirst: The head of the global recording-industry body IFPI says weakening Australian copyright protections to help AI companies train on online material would harm creators and set a damaging precedent. The government says any changes must provide meaningful control and fair compensation.

image.caption: The music industry is concerned about proposed changes to copyright rules for AI training.

sources.originalTitle: Weakening AI copyright law will spell ‘disaster for creativity’, global music body warns Albanese

segments.body: Victoria Oakley, chief executive of the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, has urged Australia not to relax copyright rules to make it easier for AI firms to train on creative work. She argues that licensing is possible and warns that a change could affect music and culture beyond Australia if other markets follow.

segments.title: A contested policy question
segments.body: The Guardian reports that some AI companies have sought an opt-out approach, under which material could be scraped unless rights holders object.
